speechtext: Then, I consider the matter closed. Resuming debate, the hon. member for Ottawa West.

Mr. Speaker, I want to start these comments today with a thank you. I want to thank all the people, and there are a quarter of a million plus of them across this country, who every day deliver services to Canadians. I want to thank the people who help my constituents in getting their unemployment insurance cheques, who help them find jobs or training programs when they need it, who help seniors process their old age security cheques, even when there are now backlogs, delays and tie-ups at offices arising from cutbacks in the public service and a cutback in services to Canadians.
I want to thank those people I have met in Atlantic Canada who go out on the ocean and risk their lives to save other Canadians and to provide much needed services to shipping and transportation. I want to thank the people in Cranbrook and the people in Vancouver whom I have met with who are working for the Government of Canada because they want to deliver services to Canadians, who are frustrated and fed up because they are not being provided with the resources to be able to deliver those services, and the managers, who are having to do more with less and know that, in fact, what they are doing less with is less.
I want to thank all those people. I do not want to name any of them because all of them feel under threat from this government. All of them feel that any expression of an open opinion on how badly this government is managing the country can lead to them being the next on the hit list.
The Liberal Party of Canada appreciates the important role the Public Service of Canada has played in the building of this nation and in progress and prosperity for Canada world-wide.
We recognize that politicians may have had the dream of a nation from coast to coast to coast, but the people who put the bricks and mortar together include the public sector, the people who work for the Government of Canada, who carry out the wishes of this Parliament.
We believe that the country only works when there is a co-operative relationship between Parliament and the employees of the Government of Canada, based on respect and a sense of fair play. That is what is being eroded here, Mr. Speaker, far more than simply the question of what happens with somebody's pay cheque next month or next year. It is a question of whether or not this country can keep functioning productively and efficiently if this government continues to insist on using its own employees as the victims, the scapegoats of its own mismanagement of the economy, social programs, international relations and everything that is important to Canada.
In a broader vein, any nation needs a co-operative partnership between government, management and labour if it is to prosper and to make progress. That multisectoral partnership is essential to our competitiveness abroad, to our ability to continue on the road of nationhood.
What we are seeing here is part of a much bigger agenda. It is not simply a question of what is in the pay envelope next week. It is a question of persuading all Canadians that they have to be satisfied with working for less, that our economy, as a result of the policies of this government is going to become an economy of lower paid, unskilled jobs. You persuade people that they have to work for less and under any conditions and yet at the same time you deprive them of the institutions that protect their rights to fair, open bargaining with their employer.
Those rights are under attack, not just for the public servants in this case, but for all Public Service employees and for all private sector employees.
September 17, 1991

I want to talk about a couple of things. First of all, the government is perpetuating the myth that somehow this has to do with the economic situation of this country. We all know who has created that economic situation, and if we ever needed more evidence, we just need to look at the way in which they are using that as an excuse in this particular case. We heard nothing in the February budget and we are hearing nothing in this debate that we have not heard for six consecutive years. In six consecutive budgets this government has said to Canadians that they should pay more taxes, accept fewer services, accept the deterioration of medicare, education, science and research in this country. Pay more but get less. The government will downsize the Public Service; it will pay them less, and they have accepted decreasing wages against inflation for many years now. They have exercised restraint.
The promise was that for all this pain, all those extra taxes, all those cuts in services, what Canadians would get was a lower deficit and a lower debt. What has happened in those six years is that the debt has doubled. Is it not time for the government to admit that it is its fault and that this program is not working, has not worked and will not work.
There are some reasons for that. The entire payroll of the union that is now on strike against this government is only 3 per cent of national spending. That is less than the $5 billion per year this government spends to contract out.
On that note I want to switch and talk about fairness. This bill that the government tabled before us yesterday demonstrates boldly, crudely, that this government has no intention of being fair, that its plans have absolutely nothing to do with fiscal responsibility or the debt or the deficit, but simply breaking the backs of its own Public Service employees.
There is an exception in this bill which says that while Public Service employees will get a zero per cent increase, our friends, all those consultants on whom we have spent billions of dollars to tell us we love the GST and ve love the green plan, and we love the government,
Government Orders
are not subject to a freeze on their costs now or in the future.
I remind people again that what we spend on those contractors is many times what we spend on these people who are now on strike against zero. Who are these people who are on strike against zero? They are not the president of Petro-Canada with a salary of over $400,000 a year who got a $20,000 raise. They are the people whose entire salary is $20,000 after 15 years with the Government of Canada. An entire salary of $20,000 gets no increase while an appointee of this government earning $400,000 gets a $20,000 increase. That is not fair and Canadians know that is not fair.
There is money for the fat cats from this government, lots of money for the fat cats, and no money for the work horses who keep this country running every day. If we ever needed proof of just how important their work is to keep this country running, we have certainly had it in the last week and a half.
This government has deliberately played politics with the fundamental infrastructure that keeps the economy of Canada running. It has deliberately provoked a strike that has disrupted transportation, disrupted the movement of goods and services, disrupted the movements of Canadians, and disrupted our social programs. The government will keep on doing that instead of accepting, as the Public Service Staff Relations Board decided yesterday, that it is breaking the law. The government can correct that and conform with the law immediately by getting back to the bargaining table, by negotiating as it should have been doing since last February and avoiding everything that is happening to this country as a result of its failure to do that.
All the government needs to do is appoint a mediator, get back to the bargaining table, and show it is looking for a solution instead of the continuation of problems.
I want to speak particularly about those who are hurt by this government's actions. While we, as members of Parliament, get our increases in a year of high inflation, while the high paid appointees of the government get their increases, while the deputy ministers and the senior managers earning over $150,000 get their increases and will even get their bonuses, their pay-offs for lay-offs, people earning $20,000 or less going down to as low as

September 17, 1991
Government Orders
$16,000, get nothing. Canadians know that that is not fair. Canadians also know that 80 per cent of the people in those lower income brackets are women.
If this bill were tested against any standard of equity between men and women, this bill would contravene the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We have other examples of inequity. We have regional rates of pay where somebody working in the poorest provinces of this country are paid less than people working in other parts of the country for doing exactly the same job. That is not equitable and that is not right.
The ministers and the members opposite keep saying: "Yes, well we will get zero too". Oh, boy, is that not nice. This year, when inflation is over 6 per cent, almost entirely due to tax increases by this government, we get our raise. But somebody earning $20,000 who cannot afford the price of bread does not get an increase. Sure, next year we will take zero when the government is projecting that inflation will be down to 3 per cent. Let us do it to ourselves when it is easy and do it to everybody else when it is tough.
The government has not been fair even among its own employees. The members opposite have said: "Other unions have accepted zero, three and three". I challenge the government to show me one contract that has been accepted at zero, three and three without other compensation to employees. The government has talked about the engineers, the air traffic controllers, the ships' officers and other groups. In every one of the contracts that has been mentioned there has been financial compensation to people for accepting zero, three and three. Either it was a lump sum payment or some shift in how wages are applied. It is upgrading a whole group by a whole classification. The government continues the unfairness because it still holds unto itself the right in this bill to change people's classification so they can say: "We are not giving them a raise. They are just getting a reclassification".
More money in your pocket is more money in your pocket, so I ask why this government is doing it for its best paid employees and not for its poorest paid employees. There is only one answer to that. Its purpose here is not to be fair, not to challenge the deficit and the debt. Canadians understand belt tightening, but they do not understand this kind of injustice and unfairness. Its
job is to persuade the lowest paid workers in the Public Service of Canada that they had better be prepared to work for this government under any conditions at any price. It is a message they are trying to get out to other workers in Canada.
Collective bargaining is a basic right in a democratic society: the right to sit down with your employer and co-operatively decide what your working conditions are going to be and what your compensation is going to be. This government has violated that right and it intends to undermine that right for every other worker in Canada.
I want to make a few other comments before concluding. Collective bargaining is in danger in Canada and when collective bargaining is in danger, then the rights of any employee, any person working for a salary in this country, is in danger.
I want to talk about who is responsible for this situation. It is certainly not the public servant who is responsible for the unemployed in this country. It is not the public servant who is responsible for putting Canadians at each other's throats. I am disgusted by what I have seen in the last week-the actions of this government putting people in a position where the grain harvest is in danger and where all segments of society are suffering simply because the government refused to talk to its employees.
This is a political fight. The difference is, nobody in this House is putting the livelihood of their family on the line. But the people who are out on strike are putting as little or as much as $1,000 in two weeks and sometimes many times that on the line because they believe they are fighting a government and a principle that most Canadians support as well. They believe they are seeing the fulfilment of the Tory agenda to disrupt yet another institution of government.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party has said they have been behind the alliance from the beginning. Well, we have taken a very strong stand against this wage freeze. We knew it would lead to this, even if the government did not. But we do not walk in here a vote the way big business tells us, like the government does. We do not walk in here and vote the way the president of any union tells us. We walk in here and vote based on what we hear from our constituents, from Canadians from the business community, from the farmers and fishermen of Canada and we say: Get a solution here.
September 17, 1991

Appoint a mediator. Stop breaking the law. Get back to the bargaining table and get services back to Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert D. Nault (Kenora - Rainy River):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know I am sitting so high up here that it is hard to see me. Hopefully, they will not put another row behind the curtains here or Pat and I will not be seen at all.
I wanted to ask my colleague a particular question that has been bothering me through this whole episode, and that is the fact that on the one hand we have been told consistently over the last seven years that the Prime Minister is the great negotiator, the individual who has the ability to conciliate with the different groups in the country and put together a package that all Canadians will accept. During that process we have also been told that the Prime Minister understands labour because, as you know, he used to do that for a living before he decided to attempt the most difficult job in the land and that is to run this country and to be the Prime Minister, the top official in the land.
I have in front of me the last 20 years of back to work legislation. I might say that it intrigues me that in the last 20 years there has been back to work legislation-all under previous Liberal governments I might add-but one of the things that interested me the most about looking back in the past and looking back at the records is that every one of these pieces of back to work legislation had the abilities for an arbitrator or a mediator put into it.
One of the things that I wanted my colleague to maybe touch on a little bit for us is why the great conciliator, the great negotiator, the present Prime Minister, did not even attempt to allow the process which we call collective bargaining to have its final conclusion. If things completely do break down there is a system which allows for an arbitrator or mediator.
I just want to quickly run by a few. In 1972 there was the St. Lawrence Ports Operations Act and it allowed for Judge Alan Gold to mediate. Again, in 1972, the West Coast Ports Operation legislation called for a mediator if no resolution was found. In 1973, Maintenance of Railway Operations Act, Judge Alan Gold again. In 1974, West Coast Grain Handling Operations Act, Dr. Neil Perry, University of Victoria, as a conciliator. In 1975,
Government Orders
West Coast Ports Operation legislation calls for an arbitrator if no resolution found. It goes on and on and on.
During the comments that I will make during my speech I will focus a little bit on these.
I would like to ask the member what her sense is as to why the present government would not attempt to do something as obvious as other governments have done in the past and learn from the institutions that we have put in place which will allow for these mechanisms to work?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. Before coming directly to an answer, I think he has raised some very important points that I hope people are keeping in mind in this. The first one is that I think the Prime Minister could be capable of negotiating. I think there has been a deliberate plan here since last February not to negotiate and, in fact, to ensure that a strike would happen and that it would be as disruptive as possible to the country. In other words, I think the government deliberately decided there would be an interruption of services to Canadians so not only is it holding its own employees hostage, but it is holding Canadians hostage.
For instance, the government clearly knew when it introduced the budget and when negotiations could have started last February it could have reasonably predicted, I think, that in September the grain elevators would be full and that the shipping of grain and the very harvest itself and the livelihood of farmers across the prairies would be in jeopardy if we were not able to move that grain. Yet the government chose not to use the power it has to designate the people working in the grain industry as essential workers. It could have done that last year. It could have done that at any time and it chose not to. To me that is a sign of a government that wants to create conflict and wants to create disruption of services to try and recoup some of its rapidly disappearing support.
I think we are also seeing a style of government here that we have seen consistently since September 4, 1984. We saw it in the free trade deal where the idea was not to bring Canadians together, but to encourage each segment of society to look only at what is good for them, not what is in the interests of the country. We have seen the promises of jobs, jobs, jobs and yet we have seen a huge

September 17, 1991
Government Orders
segment of our industrial base disappearing. When the government promised pink slips and running shoes to public servants in 1984, it did not say it also meant pink slips and running shoes for jobs, for seniors, for the unemployed and for Canadian business, but those have been the results. We are seeing the same approach as we saw in the Meech Lake Accord where it is my way or no way.
I have decided this and so you have to accept this and I think what typifies this whole approach of the government is really that horrible week in June that we all lived through when we saw provincial premiers being bullied, when we saw all kinds of psychological warfare because a few people felt that not every dot on an i, not every cross on a t in the Meech Lake Accord was perfect.
I think Canadians want leadership that is going to bring them together, not divide them, not put them at each other's throats. That is how I explain the situation we are in right now.

So, Mr. Speaker, the House of Commons is placed in the rather undesirable situation of having to debate a special back-to-work legislation reguarding the members of the Public Services Alliance of Canada.
Certainly such an outcome to lenghty and unsuccessful negotiations cannot be seen as satisfactory, and should not be for that matter, by anyone in Canada. Some accuse government of inflexibility, while others blame the union leaders, their irresponsibility and their attempts to score political points on the back of the Canadian public and their own membership.
Those who support these two conflicting philosophies will come up with all kinds of arguments to defend their position. Heaven knows that there is no shortage of them. The main problem facing us today, Mr. Speaker, is not to determine who is right and who is wrong in this conflict, and whether the government could have done more for his employees or whether union leaders have gone too far once again; neither is it to decide whether the right to strike has been trampled on, respected or abused. The main problem we are confronted with today, Mr. Speaker, is sadly our collective-and I stress "collective"-inability to restore some sanity in Canada, to set our country a logical and serene course instead of that windy and unsure road of confrontation that is destroying it.
This conflict within the public service of Canada is simply the product of excessive selfishness and individualism as well as a blatant lack of respect for authority and the law of the land. This conflict also reflects an intensive downgrading of all the values that were a source of pride for us in the past, particularly the traditional tolerance of Canadians which is increasingly giving way to intolerance.
It is altogether amusing and sad, Mr. Speaker, to see for instance how in the opinion of Quebecers Ottawa is wasting all its money in an effort to support farmers in Western Canada, how for the people of Ontario Canadians from the Atlantic provinces who fish for a living are insatiable leeches feeding on the taxes paid by the wealthier provinces, and how the people of Manitoba to this day still seem to bitterly resent Quebecers for getting these now famous contracts.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, under this public service conflict lies another Canadian reality, namely that for a majority of Canadians from wherever they live, the federal system is no longer benefitting them but only benefits their neighbours, at their expense of course.
Our nation has become-and I am very sad to have to say that-an extremely egotistical nation which fails to face reality. Our problems are rich kids problems and, more often than not, spoiled brats problems. We all demand more and more from the federal government, from our boss, from our community, from our municipality and our school board but, at the same time, we want to give less and less.
We Canadians are after short term gains, as if under the threat of an imminent world-wide nuclear war. Every budget cut made by this government or other governments in this country is met with a general outcry, thousands of dissatified voices from all parts of the country claiming that the cuts should have been made elsewhere. But if the government had the unfortunate idea of doing just that, other voices, contradictory voices would rise immediately to protest vehemently such action.

September 17, 1991

Yet the crybabies and spoiled brats that we have become want to see our $400 billion national debt eliminated or at least reduced. However, when the federal government or a provincial government bravely engages in that undertaking, no one is willing to make the necessary sacrifices.
On that subject, Mr. Speaker, quite frankly, the public service of Canada employees are no better and no worse than the vast majority of Canadians. I am disappointed, Mr. Speaker, because Canadians seem to have forgotten to take a good look in the mirror in the morning and ask themselves: "What can I do today for my country and help resolve this crisis?" Instead, Mr. Speaker, we Canadians prefer to acknowledge that a problem does exist of course but we choose to blame it on our neighbour, our boss and ultimately on the politicians, whatever their political stripe, and on any and all governments.
When it tabled the budget in February, the government had the courage to put down in black and white its strategy for economic recovery and deficit reduction. The federal government never concealed its hand from the unions or the Canadian people. Quite the contrary, it clearly stated its priorities. I find it very surprising today, Mr. Speaker, that members of the House of Commons of Canada would want to delay the passing of this back to work legislation. Each new striking day will only do more harm to all Canadians, including the strikers and their families.
It is time we as Canadians stopped playing this useless game of national self-destruction. We should stop wondering who is responsible for this strike and consider all the implications of a labour dispute that is being forced on thousands of Canadians. First of all-and this point was not brought up so far in this House, by government or opposition members, but it is a very important one-in addition to having their salaries frozen by the government in 1991, which is not very palatable to employees in the public sector, in addition to having their salaries frozen, Public Service union members are about to lose 4 per cent of their salary because their union is keeping them on strike for another week. Mr. Speaker, every week on strike means a 2 per cent drop in the annual pay of Public Service union members. This is not a cut imposed by the government but by the Public Service
Government Orders
Alliance of Canada which forced its members to go on strike.
Granted, the federal government is doing nothing this year to improve the salaries of union members, but it seems to me that today, public servants are suffering even more at the hands of their union leaders, whose strike strategy will cause them to lose even more money.
Second, the present dispute is doing serious harm to our fledgling economic recovery. Can Canada afford this useless confrontation? Third, thousands of Canadians are no longer receiving the essential services to which they are entitled. In some cases, the strike is causing very serious harm to the poorest and most vulnerable in our society.
Fourth, the unions must realize that when they work for the government, they are in a monopoly situation. When Canadians need a passport or an unemployment insurance cheque, they have to go through the federal government. Government employees should realize that the unique job security they enjoy is a benefit that does not exist anywhere else in our society.
Fifth, our fragile economy can no longer afford the kind of disruption this causes for our airlines, airports, meat inspection and grain shipping. Some unions, some union leaders and some members of the opposition have said the federal government was glad to see public servants on strike because this meant it would save several million dollars a day in salaries. That is extremely shortsighted. Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government knows perfectly well that every day of this strike costs the Canadian economy a lot more than the number of dollars saved as a result of the work stoppage.
Mr. Speaker, it is in Canada's national interest to put a speedy end to this labour dispute. This back-to-work legislation has become imperative because the strike has interrupted essential services, in addition to causing very serious harm to innocent Canadians. Our airlines, already in financial difficulty, are losing millions of dollars daily because of problems at the airport.
Canadian auto manufacturers are having all kinds of problems because the parts they need are held up at customs. Fruit and vegetables are held up at the Canadian border, and meanwhile their quality deteriorates. Our grain is not delivered on time. Canadians cannot get their passports in time for the trips they have planned. Businesses no longer receive payments owed by the federal government which annually purchases $20 billion

September 17, 1991
Government Orders
worth of goods from our businesses. This shortfall is a threat to jobs in many small businesses in Canada.
Considering these and many other reasons, I find it hard to understand why members of the New Democratic Party consider the right to strike as a supreme right in this country and refuse to entertain any negative consequences of the present situation. Instead of helping to settle this dispute, the NDP is doing its best to delay passage of special legislation and aggravate the situation.
Mr. Speaker, Opposition members are fond of making patriotic speeches about Canada and about how much they love this country. Today, Opposition members have a unique opportunity to put those grand ideas into practice and help Canada out of this crisis, instead of fanning the flames of controversy.
For all of these reasons, I think this labour dispute should be terminated today. I therefore urge all members to ask that the debate be concluded and adopt forthwith this back-to-work legislation for Public Service employees.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a very brief comment and then pose a couple of questions to the hon. member.
As I was listening to his presentation, I was wondering whether he had heard the eloquent presentation by my colleague, the member for Ottawa West, when she reminded Parliament about the role of the public servants.
I think it is clear to all Canadians that public servants are there to serve Canadians, to serve our seniors, our new immigrants, our new citizens and to serve us in Parliament as well. I would like to remind the member to keep in mind that workers would like to go back to work.
The issue before us is the process by which we would like workers to go back to work. Is it a process without honour and dignity or is it a process with honour, dignity, and with a heart on the part of this government? That is the question Canadians would like to have answered.
I suggest that if we force the workers back to work with a precondition it is almost like putting a bitter pill into a sick child, tying his hands, and gagging his mouth. That is not the way to have a child swallow the needed medicine. We have to do it with honour and respect. Likewise, we have to tell our workers that we are coming to them with a heart, that we really understand their needs. We will remove all preconditions, follow the decision of the Public Service Staff Relations Board, sit down and negotiate and appoint a mediator so that the workers can come back to work with dignity and will understand that they are valued in the Public Service.
My questions to the hon. member are these: Does he believe that the right to strike is a legal right of all Canadian citizens involved in work? What advice would he give the government so it bargains in good faith? Does he really believe in the rule of law, a law that has to be followed both by citizens and by government, particularly this government?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague from Winnipeg North for these few remarks.
In particular, he asked me whether I recognized the legal right to strike in Canada. I was the president of my union as a journalist in Trois-Rivieres, Mr. Speaker, and we had to live with an employees' strike that hurt not only the workers but also the company.
But coming back to the public sector, there is an important difference. Yes, I recognize the employees' legal right to strike. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, what concerns me about the hon. member for Winnipeg North, since he frequents the New Democratic Party members more and more, is that I think he tends unfortunately to consider the Public Service's right to strike as the supreme right that will overrule and override all other rights in Canada. That is the big problem in our society.
I did not mention it in my speech earlier, but we, especially in the Parliament of Canada, have this passion of talking about the rights of Canadian citizens, the right to strike or to do almost anything, the Charter of Rights and Freedoms that I do want to respect, but I think that all of these rights tend to make parliamentarians and Canadians forget, Mr. Speaker, that we also have re-
September 17, 1991

sponsibilities. Wherever we go, when we receive people lobbying MPs, in the two years since I was elected, Mr. Speaker, I do not remember having received a single group that came to tell me about the responsibilities that had to be faced and the difficult periods we had to go through. I do not remember seeing many like that.
On the other hand, groups have come to meet me to claim all kinds of rights, an endless list that you cannot imagine. All members of this House, be they on this side or the other, have received pressure groups telling us about their rights, regardless of the consequences for other citizens.
Mr. Speaker, I would call this the Canadian situation, this tendency we have here in Parliament only to see the rights of specific groups. I do not want to deal only with the Public Service today, but with all of them. When national organizations come to do their lobbying, they only care about their own problems, small or large. The problems of others are unimportant! They would impose on their neighbours to have their own rights recognized.
Our country is sick, Mr. Speaker, and I consider this legal right to strike in the Public Service to be one that can be exercised, but within proper limits, without imposing on other Canadians who also have rights. We all have responsibilities as well.

Mr. Speaker, I have a short comment with two very brief questions.
I note that the member discussed the saving that the government is making as a result of this strike. I believe he said something in the neighbourhood of 2 per cent per week.
Since the workers will be off for something just over two weeks, this will provide a bit of a sizeable saving, or extra funds. Was he inferring that this would mean that there would be some funds that could be available for negotiations, or does he view the government's policy as being zero increase for each and every individual? Does that zero increase only apply to the total budget?
If it does apply to the total budget, I am wondering whether we can still see some optimism for a settlement here.
Government Orders
My second question is a very brief one. I know he alluded to problems with grain movement. Was he aware of any grain movements through the seaway prior to the declaration of the strike? My information was that there was virtually nothing moving in that avenue from the prairies. It was pretty much plugged up, and because of the lack of sales it was not very likely to be unplugged.

Mr. Speaker, on the issue of grain movements, I think the hon. member from Saskatchewan could talk to farmers in his own area who are getting increasingly worried about what is going on with this strike. He is probably in a better position than I am to confirm this information. Every night, on the news, even on the French networks, we see Saskatchewan farmers greatly concerned about the attitude of the New Democratic members in this House who work in the higher interest of their Public Service union, instead of worrying about the state of the economy in Saskatchewan and all other provinces.
On the second issue, I would like to make myself clear, since I am not sure my colleague got my point. I clearly indicated that some members in this House wrongly claim this strike is making us happy, because we are saving some money. It is quite the opposite. The Government of Canada recognizes that the very small amount we can save with this strike is nothing compared to the enormous losses the Canadian economy is suffering.
Also, it is true the government is freezing wage increases at 0 per cent, even though I would have preferred to avoid any such freeze, but the government is imposing a freeze. According to the government's plan, there is zero increase. But the unions- Maybe you could talk to your friends in the civil service. These people are imposing a salary reduction of about 2 per cent of their member's annual pay for every week they strike. When this conflict is over, the federal government will have given 0 per cent to its employees and the Public Service Alliance will have imposed a salary reduction of around 4 per cent on its members, who it says are in dire financial straits.
Canadian men and women have to be told about that reality, Mr. Speaker. In my riding of Saint-Maurice, I know personally dozens of public servants who do not agree with the government's strategy because it hurts them, and I understand that, but they are even more angiy with their union leaders who dragged them into a strike that hurts them even more, although they knew

September 17, 1991
Government Orders
full well that they could not win against a government that had stated its policy veiy clearly in the February Budget. After this strike, Public Service unions will have to deal with their members who are suffering needlessly.
Instead of sitting down with the government, Mr. Speaker, and trying to negotiate non-monetary clauses and perhaps gaining something in that respect, Public Service unions impose a salary reduction on their members and prevent them from getting anything at the moment, which I think is most unfortunate.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Before resuming debate, I would like to suggest that members who wish to converse do so discreetly-I say this as a friendly suggestion-so that the Chair and our listeners can hear the speeches.
Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me extreme pleasure today to rise and talk about a topic that is veiy close and dear and near to me, an issue and an area that I dealt with on a regular basis in my work life before I became a member of Parliament. That is the area of collective bargaining and the area of collective rights for workers in Canada. I speak specifically about the union that I worked for in the railway industry before I became a member of Parliament, and that is the United Transportation Union.
I want to touch a little bit on that as I go along today and talk about this particular piece of legislation that is before us, and also about the need to understand what we are talking about here.
First of all, I would like to deal with the individual rights of workers and Canadians and to deal with it in two areas. One is the public sector versus the private sector, and the myth that seems to be being perpetuated on the other side that Public Service employees and those workers who work for the Public Service are different from the private sector employees who are out there, and who go on strike on a regular basis.
First of all, I want to talk about the fact that I believe, simply, that all workers in Canada should have rights. The problem that we are having here today is to define what those rights should be. On the one hand we have a government on this side which feels that because in the particular budget put forward by the then Minister of Finance in February, which outlined a particular program, therefore, the collective bargaining rights that Canadians have by law no longer are necessary or are no longer important because its agenda as a government should supersede that.
That, Mr. Speaker, is a big mistake to make. First of all, the collective bargaining right, the institution of organized labour, the institution of rights of Canadians will be there a lot longer than this particular government will, a lot longer than we as members of Parliament will be here, if we guard it very carefully and very sincerely.
The fear I have is that we are setting a very nasty precedent with this particular piece of legislation. Yes, strikes hurt. There is no doubt about that. That is what they are intended to do. If anybody on the other side can say to me: "You are allowed to go on strike only in good times; you are allowed to go on strike only when it does not hurt anybody else", then we have difficulty with understanding what the labour institution is all about and what the progress and process of collective bargaining and the need for that particular right of the individual worker is.
I get the sense, by listening to the members opposite, that they feel the only time an individual should have a right to strike is if it is not going to hurt anybody else. Well, if they sincerely believe that, then they should be straightforward and tell us as Canadians and workers that no one should be allowed to strike in this country because someone will be hurt.
One of the areas that has really interested me, as I mentioned in my question to the member for Ottawa West, is that the government has changed the rules of the game somewhat as it relates to back-to-work legislation. The great conciliator, the Prime Minister we have today, is well aware of the labour movement and collective bargaining. Unless he was the worst labour lawyer in the country, he should know that there is a particular
September 17, 1991

system in place that we have to follow in order to maintain the rule of law.
I want to again mention some of the different pieces of back-to-work legislation that came forward in the last 20 years. The reason I keep emphasizing these is because they also were a Draconian measure to a certain extent. I as a member believe that if you are going to say to Canadians and to workers that you have the right to strike, then tell them so. If you do not have the right to strike or there are certain areas of the economy that you cannot, as a government, accept allowing people to strike, then say so. That is what we call the services that are essential to all Canadians and we put those on the books to make sure those services will be maintained during these work stoppages.
The government, in a sneaky way, is saying to the Public Service that it, the Public Service, has no collective rights. It is also saying that the Public Service has no right to strike, because during the whole process of collective bargaining there is the ultimate. When you come to the end of the whole collective bargaining process, what is left? That is an arbitrator or a mediator. If they are suggesting with the back-to-work legislation that we have come to the end of the process of negotiation with no agreement, then we have to take a look at what the alternatives are.
The alternatives should always be maintained based on what we have done in the past. In the past, Mr. Speaker, based on the Maintenance of Railway Operations Act in 1966 it was back to work with an arbitrator, which meant that both sides would make their presentation to the arbitrator, and the arbitrator, an independent body, was a third party.
Can you imagine what it would be like if I was your employee, and I had to believe that you as a person, as a member of Parliament and as our Speaker, would be judge and jury every time I had a dispute. What we did to be fair to workers in this country and what governments put in the past was the ability to have an independent third party who does not have the ideology or the government's agenda at heart, but has the equal rights of everyone involved at heart. That is what arbitrators and mediators are for. That was in order the maintain the credibility of the system.
Mr. Speaker, what we have seen in the legislation before you today, is the complete erosion of the credibility of the system. Now, basically, this governments says:
Government Orders
"It does not matter what you say or what you want, I am going to tell you what you are going to get".
In 1966 they understood there was a big problem in the country. A lot of people were being hurt because, as you know, in those days when railroads were in their prime, when they shut down the whole country shut down. Therefore, what took place was was back-to-work legislation but the government gave both sides the legitimate right to go in front of an independent third party to make their cases and let that person rule on it.
In 1972, under the St. Lawrence Ports Operations Act, the same situation took place. In 1973, again it was the same situation with a railway strike, with Judge Alan Gold being asked to arbitrate the dispute. With the West Coast Grain Handling Operations Act in 1974, Dr. Neil Perry of the University of Victoria was the conciliator. In 1975 the legislation called for an arbitrator if no resolution was found. In 1975, again under the St. Lawrence Ports Operations Act, Judge Alan Gold was asked. In 1976, under the Port of Halifax Operations Act, again there was a court magistrate who was appointed as mediator if no resolution was found. In 1977, the Air Traffic Control Service Continuation Act, there again was the ability for an arbitrator to look at whether this dispute could be resolved. In 1978 with the Postal Services Continuation Act the mediator was the then minister. In 1978, the Shipping Continuation Act, it was William Kelly, as every one knows, as in 1982, the West Coast Ports Operation Act, with William Kelly again.
I bring forward this issue because what we have seen with the present government is a change of how we deal with disputes in the Public Service. Basically that is what the government has done, and it really interests me that it has done it. In 1966 when the government of the day, the Liberal Party, gave the Public Service the right to strike, the Progressive Conservative Party, which now governs this country, voted in favour of that. It meant at that time in 1966, when Mr. Diefenbaker was still the leader, they felt very strongly that yes, there was a right for workers in the public sector to pull their services if they felt they were being treated unjustly.
To go further with that theme, we now have something that is even worse and that is the belief by not only the workers but the decision and the belief by the Public Service Staff Relations Board that indeed this particular government has not been negotiating in good faith. I do not know if members on the other side realize how worrisome it can be to believe that even before you start the other side has no intention of coming to an agree-

September 17, 1991
Government Orders
merit. Then again we look at the complete dismantling of the institution of collective bargaining. When we look at that very seriously, we have in essence what we have seen in other countries in the world: complete chaos where we cannot maintain the rule of law because workers have lost complete faith in their governments. We may sit here and say that it would never happen in Canada because we are too democratic and we do things that are just and fair. We know the difference between right and wrong. My leader spoke very eloquently about the difference between right and wrong. When we get the Public Service Staff Relations Board telling us that what the government is doing in dealing with its own civil servants, its own employees, is wrong, then we all have fears and we should all be very fearful of what is to take place next.
It does not surprise me one little bit that the president of the alliance would come out publicly and say: "We may just ignore the law." The reason for that is simply: "If you can ignore the law, as the Parliament of Canada has done under section 51, then why should I honour the law?" That is a very serious situation to be taking place in our country. Once we let ourselves, as members of Parliament, agree that breaking the law is acceptable, whether it be under section 51 or whether it be a president of a union saying: "Well, it doesn't matter because we may just continue this anyway", we are really leading toward what we have seen in other countries and that is a complete dismantling of the institutions that we have put in place to have what is aptly put, good government.
I think I should read into the record what the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruling states. First of all, the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruled in line with decisions, and this is not new. They ruled in line with the decisions by the Ontario Labour Relations Board and the British Columbia Court of Appeal, which held that to insist on preconditions before bargaining for a collective agreement is contrary to the requirement to bargain in good faith. Here is exactly what they said in that ruling:
The insistence on conditions precedent to negotiating terms and conditions of employment at the bargaining table is incompatible with the requirement to make every reasonable effort to negotiate a collective agreement. Accordingly, the board declares that the employer has acted contrary to Section 51 of the act and orders the employer to comply with Section 51 of the act.
Well, that is pretty obvious and pretty clear. Other institutions, other provincial jurisdictions, other governments and other areas that we deal with on a regular basis, have already ruled that you cannot put preconditions. Therefore, what this is telling us is that the budget is basically a plan. The Minister of Finance puts down a budget and it is a road map to where the government is going to go. It does not mean that it is etched in stone. As one knows, the government very rarely meets its objective. It is an attempt to try and get where it wants to go-
For the minister of the Treasury Board to stand up in this place and tell us: "We told you in February that this is what we were going to do, so we have no choice but to do it" is nonsense. The fact remains, in this system we have set up, you have go to the table with the sense that we are here to look at the issues and we are here to negotiate.
Let me remind the Prime Minister, since he has probably forgotten this. I am aware that he has shut a few towns down in his day. The Prime Minister has to understand that negotiation is the art of compromise. It means that you do not get exactly what you want and I do not get exactly what I want when I go to the table. But we get what is best for both sides.
It is not right to sit here and tell anyone who has ever been involved in the labour movement: "You are going to get this whether you like it or not. Do not bother to tell me how you feel, inflation is running at 6 per cent. I do not really care. That is what you are going to get". What one is looking to find are some severe problems in the labour movement.
I was talking to my colleague about an hour ago about this particular issue. One of the things that is well known in public life is the moment you lose the faith of the civil servants, one is really in for big trouble, simply because those are the unelected people who put in place the policies of a particular government.
Simply, what it has said to the Public Service is: "You have no rights. You have no voice." Under collective bargaining, that is the only voice it has to show its employer that it disapproves of certain issues. If that is taken away, then it has to expect to get it from a different arena.
September 17, 1991

I really pity the government for what is going to take place in the next year and a half once this legislation goes through. I also must say that I expect on this side that people will be very excited to see all of these brown envelopes show up at their door on a regular basis, because now the credibility of the government has been completely undermined. I am sure the Public Service will start to undermine every move the cabinet and this government makes because they have done the same to
them.
And as we know, all is fair in love and war. Therefore, what the government has declared on the labour movement and the Public Service is war. Now it will be seen in a lot of different forms. I believe the government should be put on notice that that is exactly what it has done with this kind of legislation that does not follow the rule of law.
I want to talk briefly about the back-to-work legislation. One of the things we cannot fool ourselves about is that this is a complete suspension of collective rights. Let us not kid ourselves that this is a plan of the Tory government just to allow wage restrictions for a certain period of time. Looking at the legislation, it also has the ability to reclassify the Public Service. It claims it is just following out its mandate under PS 2000 and will continue to do that. It uses the equity that we have been working on for many, many years now, as it relates to women, as the argument in order to reclassify if it wishes. I think that is a pretty scary indication of just where this government is prepared to go.
The other issue is the back-to-work legislation. It does not deal with the contracting out situation that we are now facing in the government. If we follow what is being told to us by many, that contracting out is now at the level of $5 billion, it seems quite unfair and wrong to think that on the one hand it is okay to allow the contracting out to continue unrestricted.
Regarding the minister, who is the only minister from Ottawa, I can understand why he would be here squirming in his seat considering what this may do to his career. I would think that he may look at the minister who was
then,	in 1966, pushing forward the legislation in the belief that public employees have the right to strike. It was the member from Ottawa or the member from
Government Orders
Carleton, if I am not mistaken, and before they were thrown out of office, he was the minister responsible for the Treasury Board in the Diefenbaker government. I can understand why the minister across the way would be a little nervous.
I want to wrap up by saying this. The labour relations in this country are a very, very sensitive thing. In order for a government to be successful, two things have to happen. One is that you need to have understanding of what workers are looking for and they have to understand what you want. Second, you need to have what is most appropriate, the faith in your government that it will do the right thing.
I think that the partnership between government, labour and business has been broken and therefore we will see the complete dismantling of the rule of law under this particular piece of legislation. I think anyone of sound mind and body would have no choice but to vote against this.

Mr. Speaker, I regret the complexify of the name of the constituency, but it has a local significance.
I appreciate the opportunity to ask my hon. colleague a question, but first of all to make a comment or two. Initially I sat and listened this morning to the amendment that was made and, while I have had some previous experience in another jurisdiction consisting of some nine years and therefore it gives me some degree of expertise in parliamentary procedure, I know of no other jurisdiction that will allow an amendment that completely contravenes the intent of the original motion. I look across the way at a former municipal colleague who I know would agree with me that it makes absolutely no sense that if you disagree with a motion all you have to do is vote against it, but there seems to be some purpose in restating, re-inventing the wheel. I sit there and I listen with amusement and I hope that some day it takes us somewhere.
The hon. member opposite alluded to several issues that give a particular bent to the matter before us that I do not happen to agree with. I agree fully that this is a situation that no one takes any great deal of pride in. It is not a situation in which government members sit here with glee and delight in knowing that they are going to

September 17, 1991
have to interfere with a process that we would like not to interfere in.
The hon. member makes reference to the elimination of collective bargaining. I would suggest to him that there is not a political party in Canada that has not found itself in the same position and regretfully caused itself to legislate people back to work. I can say that having lived in Saskatchewan and having seen the NDP government of 1982 having to do exactly the same thing, not with the Public Service, but I believe it was, at that time, with the nurses.
I sit here and I listen to that knowing that everyone here, without exception, has had experience in the unpleasant task that we have at hand and I wonder where there could be such a defence against having developed the need to become involved in this insatiable requirement that is placed before us.
I would like to ask the hon. member a couple of questions. Ele indicated that he felt there was no difference between the government and the private sector. I suggest to him, for a minute, that perhaps there is some difference in that the government sector provides a service that the public demands on an ongoing basis 52 weeks a year. I would suggest that in the private sector that is not the case.
From time to time, there were certain members of the private sector losing their jobs for periods of time through lay-offs and so on, not to the same-

Mr. Speaker, thousands of Newfoundland fishermen and plant workers are facing the worst crisis they have faced for decades. For months they were unable to fish because of severe ice conditions. When many of them did get out they found there were no fish to catch. Fishermen were losing more with every trip they took.
With the fishing season for many coming to a close one simple and tragic fact is clear: thousands of Newfoundlanders are facing a very bleak winter.
I am calling on the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans to put in place a disaster relief program which will ensure that the close to 8,000 inshore fishermen who will not qualify for UI are not forced out of the fishery or on to the welfare roles of the poorest province in Canada.
The government cannot claim to have been unaware of this problem. In an internal DFO memo dated June 28, 1990, the minister was advised that the current fisheries failure may appear unprecedented, but it is probable that failures of similar magnitude could occur in the future in this or other fisheries.
There is no excuse for delay. It is time to act.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in Winnipeg on September 5, the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State announced a $158 million program, a strategy to help people with disabilities integrate into the mainstream of Canadian life. As the Prime Minister commented, what every disabled persons wants most is simply to be recognized as an individual.
It was with this understanding that the National Strategy for the Integration of Persons with Disability has been designed. The program stresses partnership between disabled persons and the community, partnerships that can overcome barriers of attitudes and of space and access that prevent disabled people from achieving their full potential.
September 17, 1991

The key word is "access" to places, to employment, to opportunity. Canadians must tear down the barriers both mental and physical and make this integration program the success that it can be.

Mr. Speaker, this morning in The Hague Lord Carrington announced that a new Yugoslavian ceasefire had been successfully brokered. At the same time the armed conflict is escalating. All parties are on the offensive. Warships are on the move. Ports are being shelled. There is even a danger that neighbouring countries may get involved.
While lives are being lost and successive ceasefires fail, my colleagues and I are being petitioned from all sides to work toward an end to the conflict. There is much to be discussed if all the people of Yugoslavia are to settle their differences and live in peace, but it is critical that the temperature of the conflict be lowered first.
While the EC and CSCE as vehicles for settling this dispute appear to be having little success, third party intervention by UN peacekeeping forces has proven successful in the past. Canada has an opportunity to show leadership on the international stage.
When will the government realize that Canada must work on a most urgent basis to support the ceasefire? We must support the request by the presidents of both Yugoslavia and Croatia for UN peacekeepers. Lives are being lost while we wait.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship; Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: NATIONAL STRATEGY FOR THE INTEGRATION OF PERSONS WITH DISABILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, persons with a disability see every day as another challenge. They are constantly up against obstacles that put them at a disadvantage when seeking employment and advancement, education and training and equal access and participation. In other words, they cannot lead normal lives. Active co-operation by federal departments with Canadian communities is helping to eliminate these obstacles.
The National Strategy for the Integration of Persons with a Disability, announced by the Prime Minister on September 6 in Winnipeg and by the Secretary of State on September 9 in Montreal, would not succeed without the partnership that exists between provincial, territorial and municipal governments.
Of course, we must not forget volunteer groups, the business community, the media, unions and disabled persons and the organizations they represent. These partnerships already exist and are growing daily.
Mr. Speaker, it is up to each and eveyiyone of us to support these partnerships and to urge all Canadians to help implement this admirable strategy.

Mr. Speaker, the tactics this unpopular government is using against its own employees are unconscienable. It brings in devious pay increases for the upper echelon of the Public Service and Crown corporations. It introduces wage controls on lower level public servants. It ignores the collective bargaining process. Promises have been broken with respect to pay equity. Untruths have been told about contracting out. All this is done in the hope that Canadians will become hostile to the strikers.
The government is in effect saying to all employers in Canada that it is okay to throw away the right to bargain and to hold over the heads of workers the threats of job losses and contracting out.
We have a government that is politically opportunistic, with no respect for the citizens of this country. It is not too late for this government to negotiate a fair solution that will put the Public Service back on its feet while generating a spirit of good will for the future.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of Parliament I am constantly confronted by mothers, fathers and children whose basic human rights are being violated. They are deprived of security of person, of physical and mental health and are subject to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment because their

families are separated, frequently for as much as six years.
I urge the minister of immigration to issue minister's permits for spouses and dependent children of persons who have been determined to be convention refugees and allow families to be reunited in Canada for inland processing as is done in the United States.
Let us cut bureaucratic processing time and cost, reduce health and welfare costs, and help families who will be Canadian citizens.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in this House the hon. government House leader, in making reference to a letter which he received, asked: "Why do we have this archaic practice of having first reading, second reading, third reading, for pieces of legislation?"
This government has proven itself capable of, in just a few years, dismantling a parliamentary system which took centuries to develop. It has steamrolled over our institutions of democracy to enact a Draconian legislative agenda which Canadians do not support, and now the minister says: "Why do we need to have all of these stages of debate in the House of Commons?" Perhaps next he will ask: "Why do we need to have the House of Commons at all?"
It seems that the government has realized that at 14 per cent in the polls the only way that it can hold on to its power is to do away with democracy and rule Canada by a dictatorship. At least one good thing might come out of it: We would not need the government House leader any more, now would we?

Mr. Speaker, self-determination is being increasingly established as the right of people in every comer of our changing world. We have seen citizens of east European countries and the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia being granted a voice in the determination of their
political futures. Unfortunately, this is not the case for the people of Croatia and Slovenia who voted 95 per cent in favour of independence.
Today, His Excellency Yves Fortier, Canada's Ambassador to the United States, has stated that on the instructions of the Prime Minister of Canada he will explore with the United Nations Security Council the possibility of establishing a UN peacekeeping force in Yugoslavia.
I know that every member of this House will join with me in supporting a role for Canada as an integral part of any effort to help put an end to the bloodshed in Yugoslavia.

Mr. Speaker, on March 15 this year, I rose in the House to discuss the economy in the Montreal area, and I recalled the passionate words spoken by Jean Marchand who always pointed to Montreal as the economic heartland of Quebec.
On Tuesday, June 4, 1991, the caucus I represent launched a one-day debate in this House on the economy in the Montreal area.
Since that time, not a single government initiative. The responsible minister prefers to ignore a situation that has become catastrophic.
On behalf of all Quebecers and the people of Montreal, I ask and beg the Prime Minister of Canada not to listen to me or to us, but to read this morning's impressive article in the Journal de Montreal by Jean-Phi-lippe Decarie, and a number of reports by that excellent journalist, Michel C. Auger. If he does, I am sure he will get rid of the minister responsible for Montreal and let him take on lesser responsibilities. I am sure he has a number of members who would be able to do the job, and I am thinking of Hogue, Tetreault, Della Noce, Gibeau and others. They will have no trouble doing a better job than the minister because, Mr. Speaker, the situation in Montreal has reached catastrophic proportions. I hope the minister is replaced by one of the members I just mentioned.

Mr. Speaker, we are all concerned about our environment.
For 10 years there has been a very successful program for controlling debris on the Fraser River, the port of Vancouver and Flowe Sound. It is the Fraser River debris program. It has been jointly funded by the federal and provincial government as well as the forest industry.
In spite of the large expenditures made for the clean-up of the Fraser River in the green plan, the debris control program appears about to be discontinued. This would be contrary to any common sense as the debris control program resolves one of the major causes of pollution in the Fraser Basin and on the south coast.
The expenditure on debris control is minimal compared to damage to the marine, fishing, tourism and recreational activities. I would plead with all the departments involved to continue their full support for this essential program.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's biggest rock star, Vancouver's very own Bryan Adams has been told by Canada's federal broadcast regulator that his newly released songs are un-Canadian.
All songs on Adams' new album Waking Up the Neighbours have been denied Canadian content status and are subject to restriction on all FM radio stations.
At the same time songs by British rocker Tonight's the Night Rod Stewart and U.S. blues singer Bonnie Raitt are considered Canadian and allowed unlimited play.
This ruling is an insult to a quintessentially Canadian performer who has received both the Order of Canada and the Order of British Columbia for his work.
Something is clearly wrong with the CRTC grading system on Canadian content when artists like Adams are denied Canadian status.
I call upon the CRTC to revise its evaluation procedures and amend this outrageous ruling. It is an insult to Adams and to all other Canadian performing artists.
Come on, CRTC. Get with it, eh?

Mr. Speaker, many of my constituents are concerned about the actions of Canada Post, especially when it comes to meaning the closure of a rural post office such as in Halton, Ontario.
Some people think the member of Parliament should directly interfere in the business operations of Canada Post, but there has to be a better way.
I call on the government to accept the advice of the House of Commons consumer and corporate affairs committee and privatize Canada Post; then set up an independent regulatory agency with decision-making powers something along the lines of the CRTC.
That way, clients of Canada Post and communities affected by it would have a way of appealing decisions made by the corporation. We would have something that is lacking today. We would have accountability.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a letter I wrote to the Prime Minister on August 27 on the situation in Yugoslavia:
We are witnessing the most intensive fighting yet in Yugoslavia's undeclared civil war.
The Yugoslavian army, controlled by the communist Serbian government, continues to ignore the Yugoslavian presidency under Stepe Mesic and attack the Croatian National Guard under the duly elected Government of Croatia.
At this time of crisis, I urge you to recognize the independent republics of Croatia and Slovenia, and to immediately ask that all Yugoslavian troops be withdrawn from Croatian territory in an effort to help curb the further escalation of the conflict.

September 17, 1991
Oral Questions
Canada's support of the independence of Croatia and Slovenia
would be viewed as our meaningful commitment to freedom and
democracy.

Mr. Speaker, last Sunday evening, Mr. Chretien stated, in response to questions from the press on constitutional issues, and I quote: "What the people of the Gaspesian Peninsula want is to get their UI cheques. They do not care whether they come from Quebec or Ottawa."
All the men and women who live in that region were shocked to hear such a thing. They will never tolerate that such a value judgement be made about their community. Contemptuous statements such as this give away the ignorance of their author concerning the history of this wonderful region and its people. The Gaspesian workers are proud, courageous and hardworking people. As a matter of fact, is it not a fact that they are one of the most valued workforce in the whole of Canada? They want to work, not to sit and wait for their UI cheques as Mr. Chretien would like us to believe.
Mr. Speaker, I call upon all Gaspesian men and women to let the Leader of the Opposition know in no uncertain terms that they absolutely find such comments unacceptable. Mr. Chretien, the people of the Gaspesian Peninsula have heard you and they will remember it in due time.

Mr. Speaker, we learned yesterday of the closure of the Canadian Pacific Angus Shops, in the east end of Montreal. Nine hundred jobs will be lost, on top of the many jobs that have already been lost in the rail and air transportation industry in Montreal. This situation is unacceptable.
What is also inadmissible for Montreal is the inaction of the Minister of Transport the very minister who unfortunately is responsible for the Montreal area. The Chamber of Commerce of Montreal denounced this
minister who refused to meet with them. Mr. Speaker, this government has lost its credibility and this minister proved to be incompetent a long time ago. Montreal deserves better that this bunch of politicians without a vision that make up this government.
My party support the sovereignty option for Quebec. As its mayor stated before the Belanger-Campeau Commission, Montreal needs a national Quebec policy to promote its development. A sovereign Quebec would have the added advantage of not imposing upon the rest of Canada-
I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time is up.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Right Hon. Prime Minister a question. A few years ago, as you drove into Montreal, you saw signs with a very appropriate slogan proclaiming Montreal a city with pride. Today, Montreal is a city with unemployment. After Air Canada and Canadian Airlines, now 950 jobs are being lost at the CPR's Angus Shops in Montreal. What a fine way, Mr. Speaker, to celebrate the 350th anniversary of the city. Mr. Speaker, I would tell the Leader of the Opposition that this government has promoted the economy of Montreal as it has promoted the economy of the country by taking very specific action to prepare people to hold high-tech jobs. I would tell the Leader of the Opposition that over the years, we passed Bill C-22 for the pharmaceutical industry, we helped Canadair, we helped Pratt & Whitney, we set up the Space Agency and the headquarters of the international environmental agency in Montreal. 83,000	net jobs on the island of Montreal, while in the previous four years, the Liberal Party presided over the net loss of 4,000 jobs.
September 17, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister.
When the government said the recession is over, we have to wonder what they are putting in the water cooler in the cabinet room. It seems that everything that the government touches these days turns to a disaster. I am almost afraid to ask it to try to do something about the economy, but there is the reality that there is 1.5 million Canadians who are looking for work today.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister what he intends to do to find jobs for these Canadians who want to work. You do not have to force them to work; they want to work.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the Opposition knows very well that positive growth was recorded in the second quarter of this year, 4.9 per cent at an annualized rate. The domestic demand went up by 6.9 per cent. Exports were up by 22 per cent. The merchandise trade balance is up to $12 billion. Labour income is up 5.7 per cent. Corporate profits are up by 40 per cent, and personal disposable income is up by 6.3 per cent.
The recovery began one-quarter earlier than we had anticipated. It is important to get the fundamentals right. It is important to ensure that we nip the inflationary psychology in the bud, and we have done that. We are on the road to sustainable growth and sustainable recovery with price stability. That is our goal and that should be the goal of the Leader of the Opposition as well.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):

Oral Questions
where there are hundreds of thousands of people who have lost their jobs in the manufacturing sectors. Go back to your own provinces in the west and ask the farmers what they think of the policies of this government.

The reason that we do not follow Liberal economic policy is the fact that ten years ago today the unemployment in this country was 12.8 per cent, and today it is 10.6 per cent. Ten years ago today, following Liberal economic policies, the inflation rate was 12.9 per cent. Today, it is 5.8 per cent. Ten years ago today the prime interest rate was 22.75 per cent. * sk *

Mr. Speaker, a government that stands in the House and brags about double digit unemployment is a government that has lost touch with the people. Why don't you go to the people and ask them what they think?
My question is for the Prime Minister. In his first speech those many years ago, the Prime Minister said: "Another component of industrial progress has to be a major commitment to civilized labour relations in this nation. You learn about it from those who have grown up in the area and understand the problems of living, breathing people, those who have worked out problems and have a track record to deal with, not governments that unilaterally bring in legislation"-
I would ask the hon. member to put her question.

September 17, 1991
Oral Questions
in legislation to abuse collective agreements-does he do today what he found so offensive in 1983?

But, Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to rise to tell my hon. friend indeed that was a fine speech that I gave back in 1983.
