The NDP laughs. They should be talking to the NDP government in Ontario. There is a serious strike going on in Toronto. In point of fact, there are 3 million people-
Oh, oh.
The right hon. Prime Minister.

Mr. Speaker, we have reduced very considerably the number of days lost in the Public Service and in Canada over the last seven years.
From time to time we all encounter difficult circumstances; the country is encountering a difficult circumstance now. The economic recovery is in train. It appears to be broadly based, but it remains fragile. All elements of the economy including the Public Service and the private sector have been asked and will be asked to do their very best to make a contribution to making sure that this economic recovery remains durable so that all Canadians, including public servants can benefit from a strong economic recovery in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the government's lowest paid clerks, those people who really need our help, make $16,500. A month before this Draconian legislation was brought in, that minister and that Prime Minister got a deal which will increase their compensation by $11,413 respectively.
If the government's program is so fair, why did the Prime Minister get an increase that is ten times higher than that of the lowest paid civil servants across this land?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member has her numbers wrong.
Again.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
She mixes apples and oranges. If you want to look at the Public Service in the same way, in the newspaper last week you could see that the travel budget of public servants for last year was $500 million. Should you put that in their pay? It has nothing to do with it.
The increase to members of Parliament was 3.7 per cent and to PSAC members was 4.8 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
This morning the government responded to the Public Service Staff Relations Board ruling that this government had been bargaining in bad faith, with the statement that it will go back to the negotiating table.
Oh, oh.

I suggest that the government read the ruling. The statement of the minister this morning was that the government would go back to the table with no preconditions.
It is interesting that the Minister of Finance said in his response to an earlier question that labour income in this country has gone up 5.7 per cent. He was citing this as an indication that the recession is over. For public servants this government is offering them zero per cent. The recession is not over for them.
The minister said this morning that he will go back to the negotiating table with no preconditions. Can the Prime Minister confirm that that is his government's position, that he will do that, and that his government will bargain in good faith with workers now with no preconditions?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the hon. leader of the NDP understands that the situation for these employees is difficult enough without making it a charade. It is not true that we have offered to go back without preconditions. We have always been ready to negotiate with the Public Service Alliance, as we have with others.
She will remember that it is Mr. Bean after the budget who said: "This is going to be a political strike. We want to go after this government". We sat with him for 90 days and we tried to make a deal on all of these issues that are of concern to her and to us, and he would not move.
September 17, 1991

Oral Questions
The Public Service Staff Relations Board stated what we should have done according to section 51: not bargained. We have bargained. It is not that we did that in bad faith, not at all.
They said that the board concluded that the preconditions were incompatible with the requirements to make every reasonable effort. I said that I was surprised, because we have made efforts and we are prepared to continue with those efforts. That is what I said this morning. We are prepared to sit with the union and negotiate without preconditions, but I will say that the zero, three and three is still a firm commitment.

Mr. Speaker, it is clear that there is a double message to the workers of this country. The minister has made a clear statement that he would negotiate without preconditions.

Further to the Minister's comments on negotiations with the Alliance, is the Minister now prepared to withdraw the government's challenge of the Canadian Human Rights Commission's decision on pay equity for Canadian women and for the Alliance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you allow me, the government is going to court only to obtain a formal opinion on the interpretation of a clause.
Parliament passed a pay equity law, we respect it and we are in fact the first government to set aside a sum of money, $317 million, and to set aside $80 million a year to help women achieve equal pay.
Now we disagree with the tribunal on an interpretation which we think goes beyond the law. We are prepared to comply with the court's decision, but we are asking for its opinion. That is all, nothing else. We are ready to act on equal pay; we have shown it more than any other government.

Mr. Speaker, I did not think that in order to implement the law you had to wait for a court decision. If the law is pay equity, implement pay equity. It seems to me that is the simple thing to do.
The government has talked about negotiation but the back-to-work bill remains under discussion today. I want to ask a question of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who has recently returned from a trip abroad where she spoke in Ukraine about Canada's good international record on democracy and on democratic rights and freedoms.
I would point out to the minister that the legislation put forward by this government, this back-to-work legislation, is once again legislation that is in direct violation of the United Nations Labour Convention No. 87, which guarantees freedom of association and which Canada has signed.
How can the Secretary of State for External Affairs justify making such comments outside the country and yet support her government in such legislation which contravenes the rights of workers within this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gilles Loiselle (President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of State (Finance)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the case of the Liberals I have some hope because they will have a convention, I believe, in November to start knowing what they think.
Six governments in Canada have imposed pay freezes. Liberal governments have legislated them. We have tried to negotiate them. We have sat with the unions to try to improve the package because there are a lot of other things in a collective agreement besides salaries. I may say to the hon. member that indeed we are continuing this. I have instructed my officials to inform Mr. Bean that we are prepared to sit and discuss these things with him. I am happy to inform her that indeed we are presently moving in the right direction.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
As we speak, another major blockade by Canadian truckers of the Ambassador Bridge is currently under way in Windsor, Ontario, in direct and justified response to this government's complete inaction toward the trucking industry.
I ask the minister: How many more studies, protests and blockades need to occur before the government changes the existing rules and regulations which now place Canadian truckers at a severe disadvantage to their

September 17, 1991
Oral Questions
counterparts in the United States? Do you care about protecting Canadian jobs or not?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member opposite knows very well that a task force on trucking has been at work for many months and has come to some conclusions as a result of a number of meetings.
We have met with the truckers, although the vast majority of the trucking problem rests with the provincial legislatures because they are the ones that are crucifying trucking with their very high cost on fuel. This is where the problems rest mainly.
Nevertheless, we have met with the truckers who want to speak, not with the truckers who are trying to do same thing that some people have tried to do with PSAC and turn this into a fight against the government. We are working with the truckers who want to work toward a proper solution.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians do not want to fight the government but they want to fight to protect their jobs. There is nothing wrong with doing that when a government is blind and insensitive to their pleas.
I return to the Minister of Transport. After a year and a half of promises, why has the government failed to respond tangibly to this crisis? How can it possibly sit back while Canadian truckers' families are losing their livelihood, their jobs, their savings, their homes and finally their dignity? Doesn't this government care?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is evidently not trying to work to improve the lot of the workers. He is trying to make political gains out of that. He should know by now that the studies that were commended by the task force on trucking issues have determined very precisely that the federal government taxation system has nothing to do with the problems of the truckers.
Their problems are in the provincial legislatures where the taxation on fuels is enormous, whilst at the federal level our excise tax on diesel fuel that is used by the truckers is less than in the U.S. Our excise fuel tax in Canada is 4 cents per litre. In the U.S. it is 6.2 cents per litre.

Mr. Speaker, the 1991 fishing industry along the northeast coast of Newfoundland and Labrador will be recorded as disastrous, potentially the worst in memory.
My question is for the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans. When can we expect an implementation of an aid package that will address this depressing and devastating situation?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I answered yesterday, the government well knows that we have had a very poor fishery along the northeast coast of Newfoundland and Labrador this year.
The government instituted an aid program last June and paid compensation to fishermen who were prevented from fishing by ice from May 15 to when the last of them received assistance in August. We are now considering and deciding with the provincial government and after a consultation with the industry and the union what further steps may be needed to assist fishermen and plant workers who will not be able to even secure their qualifications for UI this year.
This matter is under very active consideration. If we act as generously as we did with respect to ice compensation, then the hon. gentleman need have no fears about the assistance that will be forthcoming.

Mr. Speaker, this aid package that is going to be produced when the government is ready may have been okay for years past when the fishing industry was in trouble, but right now, when we are looking at less than 50 per cent and in some cases in various ridings 10 per cent and 5 per cent of the ordinary catch, I would suggest that these are not ordinary conditions for fishermen and plant workers who are having their incomes wiped out and not enough work to qualify for unemployment insurance. Therefore it requires emergency and extraordinary measures.
Why will the minister not give urgency to this pressing matter and come to the rescue of those in dire need, not next month, not next week, but now?
September 17, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are now in the middle of September and the fishing season is not yet over. Fish are still being caught. We are contacting every community and every fish plant along the northeast coast and Labrador to see exactly what the situation is, what the accurate, factual situation is.
We know of course that in places like Labrador it is an absolute disaster and that in areas like Black Tickle they hardly caught a dozen fish this year where they caught thousands of tonnes last year and the previous year. There are certain areas which will have to be assisted, and they will be.
We are not ready yet to announce any plan. We are talking to the provincial government which also has a heavy responsibility here and there will be an announcement in due course.

Mr. Speaker, protests across this country are mounting and spreading against this government. In Windsor and elsewhere in Ontario hundreds of truckers are blocking border crossings. They are blocking highways. They are doing so to support PSAC and to call for the resignation of this Prime Minister.
The Minister of Transport promised short-term help to truckers in July. Why has the Minister of Transport not come through with this help? Why has the Minister of Transport ignored the precarious economic situation, the grave difficulties of many Canadians across this country? Why has he not given these people the shortterm help he promised in July?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that this government has given not only short-term help to the truckers but very long-term help. By introducing the GST we have reduced taxation bill of the trucking industry by $400 million a year.

Hear, hear.
Oral Questions

In addition to that, truckers who are not blockading to support PSAC or any other political motive have sat down with us on numerous occasions to try to iron out their temporary problems.
We have worked out some solutions with them. We have indicated to them again that the main focus of their problem is in the provincial legislatures, but we are also working with them on temporary solutions. We are doing that very remarkably, to the satisfaction of the truckers, the shippers, and the owner-operators. However, those who are blockading because they want to achieve some political motives are not serving the trucking business.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Minister of Transport.
I want to remind the minister that it was his government that deregulated the trucking industry in this country, thereby setting the scene for the crisis we are in today in that industry.
The minister clearly promised in July some interim assistance separate from the impacts of the GST. What the truckers want to know is when they are going to find out what that assistance is so that they can get on with their lives, move goods on behalf of Canadians and keep the economy rolling.

Mr. Speaker, the truckers know very well what we are offering. We have sat down with them on numerous occasions. We are working toward a solution and the truckers are very happy, but they have come to realize through the process again that the main thrust of their problems is in the provincial legislatures.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:

We lost thousands of jobs in refineries, at Canadian Steel Foundries, Vickers, Air Canada, Angus, Nationair, in textiles, and the list is too long to mention them all here, Mr. Speaker. When will the minister finally convince his

Oral Questions
colleagues of the Conservative Party to find a solution to the economic stagnation in Montreal?

I believe we have no lesson to learn from people who devastated Montreal's economy and who caused so much damage to the country's economy that we have no other choice today but to take measures to redress it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as minister responsible for the economy of Montreal, this minister ought to know that Montreal used to come first for transport and high technology. Now, all major industries are dying out.
Is the minister planning to make another Schefferville out of Montreal? Will he stop referring to the 50s and start proposing once and for all a recovery policy for Montreal?
Jean Corbeil (Minister of Transport): Mr. Speaker, I think that what must be listed here is the number of initiatives that we have taken precisely to ensure that in the years to come, workers in Montreal, men and women, will continue to hold high technology jobs.
I will only mention the $65 million National Defence contract that we have been giving to the Canadian Arsenals since 1988, the contracts for almost $200 million that Spar Aerospace Ltd has received for the Canadian Space Agency, and the $86 million contract that we have given to Bombardier for the maintenance of CF-18s. Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Prime Minister. The answer from the minister responsible for the City of Montreal clearly shows that their program is one of inaction. The Quebec
Minister of Industry, Mr. Gerald Tremblay, on the contrary, understands the problem and supports a totally different position: We need to intervene in a very forceful way, he said, and I quote: "Either we take the necessary measures to build an economy for the future or we watch powerless our society becoming poorer and poorer."

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for LaSalle-Emard should, at least, have the decency of not contradicting himself in a speech of a minute and a half. He said, rightfully, that we should do something and he quotes the Quebec Minister of Industry. I just mentioned, Mr. Speaker, a large number of initiatives taken by our government regarding high technology industries that greatly helped the Montreal area. I didn't name them all, Mr. Speaker, because I didn't have the time, but over the last three years, we spent $35 million to help new industries settle in the East of Montreal which resulted in the creation of 2,000 jobs and the investment of at least $100 million by the private sector in this field alone. These are a few concrete examples, Mr. Speaker, of what we are doing to stimulate the economy in the Montreal area.

What are you talking about? Mr. Speaker, just yesterday 3,000 jobs were lost in Montreal. This is just rhetoric! Let me quote minister Tremblay again: "Choices have to made urgently. We know what the choices are. I for one have decided for Quebec."
This question is also for the Prime Minister. What is he waiting for to make an economic decision about Montreal, about Quebec, about Canada. No further studies are required. Government has the power, but it lacks the will to use it!

Mr. Speaker, it is really incredible! Understandably so, considering it is coming from a carpetbagger who in 1988 landed on Montreal Island and suddenly discovered Montreal and the province of Quebec. It takes a lot of gall on the part of a member from a party whose former leader massacred Quebec, Mr. Speaker, and excluded it from the Constitution, to come and tell us that the present leader of the Conservative Party did nothing for Quebec when
September 17, 1991

in fact he has been the only Canadian Prime Minister in the past fifty years to really stand up for Quebec!
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice and it concerns the David Milgaard case. Mr. Milgaard is one of Canada's longest serving prisoners.
The Prime Minister recently told Mr. Milgaard's mother that he would speak to the minister about the case which, if I may say, was a very decent and humane reaction.
Has the Prime Minister done that? Has the minister decided to act in what appears to be a situation where justice is not only not done, but there appears to be compelling evidence that Mr. Milgaard did not commit the crime?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:

The Prime Minister did in fact meet-

speechtext:

Oral Questions
I have already dealt with one application by Mr. Milgaard under section 690 of the Criminal Code. I have refused the application. My reasons have been made public. speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I would like to remind the hon. member that this is a process that did result in a new trial for Donald Marshall, and I have granted applications under section 690 of the Criminal Code.
It is a power that is exercised pursuant to the royal prerogative of mercy. I recognize that there are some concerns about it in the sense that it is not by definition a transparent process. I am discussing with my department ways in which in fact it could be made more straightforward.
I think it is important to emphasize that in reviewing these cases the Department of Justice has no vested interest in the outcome. Our interest is only in doing what is just.
Unlike others who wish to comment on these cases, I am confined to the evidence that could be put before a court. When in the previous application of Mr. Milgaard people were making what I considered to be highly unfair attacks on the credibility of the process, I went outside the Department of Justice to get independent

September 17, 1991
Oral Questions
advice from one of Canada's leading criminal lawyers and retired justices of the Supreme Court of Canada.
I am quite open to suggestions to make the process more-
I think we should really move on.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance who is well aware that the high value of the Canadian dollar is killing our manufacturing exporters.

If the minister has not told the governor that as yet, will he undertake to do so without delay?

The interest rates in Canada have dropped by five and one-third per cent since its high of last year. The spreads have narrowed considerably from well over 5 per cent to less than 3 per cent, so that spread has narrowed and is continuing to narrow. There are some positive results that are occurring as a result of that lowering of interest rates and the easing of monetary conditions.
The problem is that we have to continue the fight against inflation to ensure that bringing inflation and inflationary pressures down will result in a further reduction in interest rates, and that is the track that we are on.
I think that the hon. member would agree that the economy is in recovery. We expect that recovery to continue into the second half and on into next year. That will produce positive benefits for all as it has in the house building industry, as it has in the automobile industry, and as it has in confidence both within-

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Agriculture.
The P.E.I. potato industry has been seriously damaged by a supposed presence of a virus which has prevented it from exporting to the rest of Canada and the United States.

case?

Mr. Speaker, normally I would rise in my place with regard to this point of privilege under the provisions of a point of order. But I believe one can justify a question of privilege on the grounds that a remark was broadcast across the country which elicited angry telephone calls as a result. The remark tended to place, I believe, the whole House in disrepute.
I am referring to the exchange between the hon. member for Hamilton East and the hon. member for Burlington. While the hon. member for Burlington was taking his seat, a comment was made in a veiy uncomplimentary fashion, which I will not repeat on the floor of the House of Commons, but I do have a copy of the tape which I would like to review.
Again, I repeat my remarks that I rise on a point of privilege with regard to the exchange which took place

September 17, 1991
Privilege
between the hon. member for Hamilton East and the hon. member for Burlington. When the hon. member from Burlington was taking his seat, some very uncomplimentary remarks were made which I have on a tape that I would like to review.
In point of fact, I wish to refer to three short, succinct citations which I believe ought to be considered by you as justifying a point of privilege.
I quote from "Breeches and Contempts" by Maingot, Parliamentary Privilege in Canada on page 213:
To constitute a breach of privilege a statement reflecting on the conduct of a member in his capacity as a member need not to be true but it must tend to lower the House in the eyes of the public.
I suggest that the tape will prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that it does; second, there are actions which, while not directly in a physical way obstructing the House of Commons or the member, nevertheless obstruct the House in the performance of the functions by diminishing the respect to it.
The second citation which I would ask you to review, Mr. Speaker, and which I will table with the clerk, is on page 214 from the same text:
Contemptuous references hold the member in disrespect of his parliamentary conduct and, thus, the House is held in disrespect. The House of Commons is prepared to find contempt in respect of utterances within the category of libel and slander and also in respect of utterances which do not meet that standard.
The final citation is from the sixth edition of Beau-chesne, page 143, citation 486, which reads in part:
It is impossible to lay down any specific rules in regard to injurious reflections uttered in debate against particular members or to declare beforehand what expressions are or are not contrary to order. Much depends upon the tone and manner and intention of the person speaking.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will give careful consideration to what was said and the tone in which it was said.
Further quote:
Sometimes upon the person to whom the words are addressed, as whether that person is a public officer or a private member not in office, or whether the words are meant to be applied to public conduct or to private character, and sometimes upon the degree of provocation which the member speaking had received from the person alluded to. All of these considerations must be attended to at the moment as they are infinitely various and cannot possibly be foreseen in such a manner that precise rules can be adopted with respect to them.
Those are the three citations that I give to you Mr. Speaker and to the Clerk. A copy of the tape I give for you to review, and if you find that there is a prima facie case of privilege, I would be prepared to move the appropriate motion.
I stand in my place raising this because it has been the government House leader in the last 24 hours who has demonstrated to the House that he is concerned about the conduct of all members of Parliament. I wish to tell this House that after the remark made by the hon. member for Burlington, phones have rung in our offices on Parliament Hill calling to our attention the words which were used by the hon. member. I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will give careful consideration to the evidence that I put before you, and I would ask as a courtesy that you would hear the hon. member for Hamilton East who was the victim of what I believe to be a slanderous remark by the hon. member opposite.

Mr. Speaker, frankly if it were just a battle between myself and the member for Burlington I would not bother to waste the time of the House in bringing attention to it. This is not the first time that he has used disparaging comments when they relate to women members, and I refer to the time he was forced-
